sub: Technology block (d): Command Query Responsibility Segregation

title: What Is CQRS?
desc: Split the write side from the read side — and optimize each on its own

items: CQRS separates the responsibilities of commands (write operations) and queries (read operations) into two distinct models
The write model guards consistency and business rules
The read model is shaped purely for fast, convenient queries
Both are synchronized — often through events on a message bus (see Module 9)

body.alt: CQRS flow: write requests persist to the write DB, change data capture feeds a message bus, a transformation service builds the read store

title: CQRS in Air Traffic Control
desc: An ATC system processing airspace information — the textbook fit

rows: No second clearance in the same volume and time — the 409 from Module 7
Activate a temporary restricted zone (NOTAM, M12)
Every clearance inside the zone is revoked, exactly once
Current airspace picture for a zone
Answer in milliseconds, for hundreds of screens at once
Conflicts predicted in the next five minutes
Read-only — may never slow down a clearance

items: The write model stores the current state of the airspace and guarantees all data stays consistent
The read model serves fast airspace queries without putting load on the write model
Controllers get instant situational awareness; clearance processing keeps its transactional integrity

title: The Two Sides in Code
desc: The ATC example from the previous slide, reduced to two handlers

body.code: // COMMAND side — guards invariants, answers only "accepted or not" @PostMapping("/clearances") void issue(@RequestBody IssueClearance cmd) { var zone = repo.load(cmd.zoneId()); // current write-side state zone.issueClearance(cmd); // business rules live HERE repo.save(zone); // events -> bus (Module 9) } // QUERY side — zero rules, the view was built when events were projected @GetMapping("/airspace/{zoneId}") AirspaceView view(@PathVariable String zoneId) { return readStore.findView(zoneId); // pre-built, index-shaped }

items: All the business logic sits on the write side; the read side is a lookup — that is what makes it fast
The bus between them is Module 9's topic; the lag between them is the trade-offs slide coming up
Runnable version: the event-sourcing-spring-boot repo linked on the previous slide

title: Event Sourcing in 60 Seconds
desc: The write side stores what happened, not what is — and everything else is derived

body.code: // the event log — append-only, never updated ClearanceRequested { zone: "EDDS-CTR-S", drone: "mini4-01", at: 10:15:02Z } ClearanceGranted { zone: "EDDS-CTR-S", drone: "mini4-01", until: 10:45:00Z } ClearanceRevoked { zone: "EDDS-CTR-S", reason: "NOTAM A0195/26 GPS UNREL" } // current state = fold over the events state = events.fold(Zone.empty()) { s, e -> s.apply(e) } // the read model is just one more subscriber of the same events (M9 topic)
body.note: CQRS does not require event sourcing, and event sourcing does not require CQRS — but they pair naturally: the events that keep the two models in sync are the log.

items: The log is the audit trail: after an incident, every clearance decision is reproducible — the verification evidence Module 3 asks for, by construction
Replay: rebuild a read model from scratch, or re-run yesterday's traffic through new conflict logic — Kafka's offset rewind from Module 9 is the same idea one layer down
The price: old events never change, so their schema must be versioned; long streams need snapshots to keep the fold fast
List the events FLY MISSION (Module 5) emits — TakeoffCompleted, LegFlown(distanceM, headingDeg), TurnCompleted, Landed, MissionAborted(reason), …
Which of them does a where is the drone now view need, and which only a what did it do view? That split is the two read models of project idea #11

title: What CQRS Buys You
desc: Four concrete gains — each one measurable in the ATC example

items: ✔ Independent scaling — a thousand map clients read the airspace; a handful of operators write to it. Two loads, two models, two deployments
✔ A read model shaped like the screen — the airspace view is pre-joined and pre-sorted: one lookup, no transactions, no locks in the way of a controller's query
✔ A small, auditable write side — every state change goes through one command handler where the rules live; reviewing safety logic means reviewing that one place
✔ Freedom of technology — a relational store for commands, an in-memory or geo-indexed store for queries (the moving map in Module 14 wants the latter)

title: CQRS Trade-offs
desc: The pattern is powerful — and it charges for it

items: ✘ Complexity — separating read and write models complicates the system: synchronization mechanisms become mandatory infrastructure
✘ Cost — multiple databases and a split codebase raise development and maintenance effort
✘ Eventual consistency — read data lags write data by design; brief inconsistencies are possible
In a critical environment like flight monitoring, that lag needs explicit countermeasures: staleness indicators, bounded lag monitoring, fallback to the write model for safety-relevant queries
Use CQRS where read and write loads genuinely diverge — not as a default architecture
CQRS splits one model into a write side that guards rules and a read side shaped for queries — synchronized by events on Module 9's topic
Event sourcing stores the events themselves; state is a fold over the log — audit trail and replay come for free, schema versioning and snapshots are the bill
The gains are concrete: independent scaling, a screen-shaped read model, one auditable place for safety rules
The cost is eventual consistency — in flight monitoring, make the lag visible and bounded, never silent
Project idea #11 builds exactly this for the drone: mission commands on one side, current and historical state on the other
